Inquiry was made a few days ago as to the damage to the Library. I asked for a report from the Joint Librarians, and the report reached me to-day. I think.it desirable to read it for the information of members:
Library of Parliament,
Ottawa, February 14, 1916.
Sir,-In response to your request for a report on the condition of the Library and the losses sustained by the fire of Thursday night, February 3, we have the honour to report as follows:
Some exaggeration prevails as to the extent of the loss sustained. During the night of the fire, in accordance with instructions from the chief of the fire brigade, a large number of volumes were removed by the library staff, and by the troops kindly and promptly offered by Colonel Street, of the 77th.
These were stored in various places and the volumes that had to be left partly in the open were protected by the men of the Public Works Department as well as was possible.
Later in the night the removal was countermanded by chief of the fire brigade. The last load of these books so removed was returned on Thursday, February 10. There has therefore not been time to re-arrange the books and ascertain the loss in removal and the damage by water.
Our actual total loss by fire is certainly large, but is confined to books in the reading room and gallery above, as follows:
1st. An extensive collection of rare editions of the Bible.
2nd. A very large collection of English pamphlets.
3rd. A still larger collection of reviews magazines and periodicals of various kinds: Quarterly, monthly and weekly, both French and English.
4 th. A valuable collection of ecclesiastical literature and law covering more than a century.
5th. Some valuable scientific encyclopedias and dictionaries in the French lan-[DOT] guage.
6th. A great number of valuable donations from the Imperial Government such as the Rolls series, etc.
7th. A fine collection of the reports of the American Bar Association obtained at considerable cost not long ago.
In the course of time, and when space can be available again, the Librarians consider that the most of these losses can be repaired, through the usual library agencies, without departing from the customary routine of business, and without making undue, if any, demands on the Treasury.
Especial attention is directed to the little damage done by water. Though many millions of gallons of water covered the floor and poured out through the doors from Thursday

night to Sunday afternoon, hardly any found its way to the basement, a testimony to the honest work done by the contractors in 1876, when the Library was constructed.
Those volumes that were at all damaged by water have been placed in a position to be dried; and little fear is felt that many will be destroyed. Some rich volumes of illustrated works of the 18th century may be soiled, but at-present we know of none that will be ruined.
If exaggeration prevails as to our losses, no praise can be exaggerated in being bestowed on the work bf the Library staff on the occasion of the fire.
Mr. Hamlyn Todd, whose name is traditionally associated with the Library, was fortunately able to force his way through the cordon of military and police, and got access to the Library by the side door, in time to exhibit his usual energetic disposition and capacity in raising the lower tiers of books from the water and in directing the operations of the removal of the books by the military and messengers.
Mr. MacCormac, who was present at the outbreak of the fire, promptly had the iron doors leading into the corridor - closed against the on-rush of smoke and flame. He was probably instrumental in saving the lives of some members who were in the Library by refusing to open the doors and by sending them safely through the side door, usually kept locked and bolted since the police took charge of the buildings.
Two others of the staff, Messrs. Meiklejohn and Argue,-, who were present rendered most valuable and intelligent service on the occasion ; and since the fire and after access was had to the Library, all the staff have been most industriously and intelligently engaged in restoring order.
The clerks in charge on the occasion personally desire that credit should be given to the firemen, to the soldiers of the 77th and to the. police for the effective assistance volunteered and rendered.
The librarians are requested by Mr. Todd to particularly thank Mr. Controller Fisher and Mr. Harry Stewart who were at once able and willing to render service on the occasion.
At such a time of terror and confusion, it is gratifying to report that all who were present on the occasion, or who were able to obtain access to the Library were able to be of service in an unaccustomed and nerve-racking emergency.
Some complaint was felt and made concerning the strictness of the cordon which was kept about the Library preventing the access of those who might have been of some use. But on reflection, the librarians are bound to say that the soldiers and the police could not have been expected to discriminate among persons they did not know, and that in carrying out their orders to the best of their knowledge, they were but doing an obvious duty.
We have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servants,
A. D. DeCelles,
General Librarian. Martin J. Griffin,
Parliamentrry Librarian.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1.	The Government is informed that the British and French Governments have purchased horses in'Canada for army purposes since the first of August, 1914. I understand also that the French Government is buying horses in Canada at the present
[DOT] time.
2.	The British Government has not been purchasing horses for some months; I think since about November. I would not feel at liberty to give information to the House as to the number of horses purchased as it would be against the policy which the British Government has pursued in such

matters. The British Government does not give information as to the numbers of horses, or munitions, or anything of that kind which they purchase.
3.	Representations were made to the Government of Great Britain with regard to the number of horses obtainable in Canada, and the British Government was asked to communicate these representations to the French Government. The result was that in August last an arrangement was made between the British Government and the French Government, by which the French Government should be permitted to purchase horses in this country.
4.	The Government is not aware whether the British and French Governments are purchasing horses in the United States for army purposes.
5.	The Canadian Government stopped
purchasing horses for the reason that an arrangement was made during the past summer by which the British Government would purchase whatever horses might be necessary, not only for the British forces but for the Canadian forces as well. That arrangement was made in the early part of August, and I believe that since about that time the Canadian Government has not been purchasing horses for military purposes.	x

speakeroldname: Mr. W. B. NORTHRUP (East Hastings) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the procedure under which divorces are granted by Parliament, and the consequent unreasonable expense thereof, are so unsatisfactory, besides being prohibitive to the great majority of the people of Canada, the same should be taken into immediate consideration by the Government during the present session, with a view to reform.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when., two years ago, I brought this same motion before the 
House, I thought its wording was sufficiently clear to prevent any possible misunderstanding. There are two questions which can be raised with regard to divorce. The one is, as I have pointed out before, and as I may point out again, with regard to extending the grounds on which divorce should be granted, and I am sure that a casual reading of the motion will show that it in no way refers to that. The other ground is one which I would have thought conclusively and clearly set out: that the present procedure is not satisfactory, that it is unreasonably expensive, and that it is prohibitive to a great portion of the people of this country, and consequently fails to be effective. One would think, as I thought then, that there would have been no hesitation on the part of this House to remedy such an acknowledged evil. But to my surprise, when the House came to the discussion of this question on the last occasion, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) made a speech, eloquent, argumentative, perfectly .sound and unanswerable as to the point at which it was directed, bht it was a point that had not been raised by the resolution before the House. If my motion had been to extend the grounds on which divorces were granted I could have understood the pertinency of the hon. gentleman's remarks, but inasmuch as I carefully pointed out that I was not even remotely referring to that, I confess it seemed to me that his observations, however admirable, were not pertinent to the question before the House.
When the right hon. the Prime Minister came to discuss the question he, as a perusal of Hansard will show, entirely agreed with me, that the present procedure is not satisfactory. It is not only not satisfactory, but if one were speaking outside of the walls of Parliament one would say it was absolutely idiotic that men living in the twentieth century and claiming to be civilized should consent to have such an important matter carried on as it is carried on in the Dominion of Canada. When the right hon. gentleman had agreed with me that the procedure was unsatisfactory, as every member of this House must admit, a motion was made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard) in these words:
A committee of seven members to be appointed to inquire into the existing procedure under which divorces are granted, and to report whether any and what more satisfactory procedure should be provided in such cases.
Personally, I had no. objection to that motion, assuming it to be made in good

faith, and therefore I did not oppose it. Really the only difference between my motion and it was that my motion called upon the Government as a Government to take proper steps to do away with a distinct evil, while the motion of the hon. member for Victoria, without differing from mine in principle, merely asked that a committee of seven should be appointed. I had no objection to that, and I have no objection to it to-day, if the committee would honestly and practically proceed to do its work. But after several members of the House had joined in the discussion, the right hon. the leader of the House moved the adjournment of the debate, which everybody .knows meant that my motion went to the foot of the Order Paper, and that was the last heard of it during that session. What has been done since? Last year I again placed the motion on the Order Paper, but that being a war session I did not wish to press it, and I was in hopes that the Government would take steps. I understood that some step was to be taken, and a step was taken.
In order to meet this evil, which no member of the House pretended to say did not exist, for the proceedings were ridiculously cumbersome, absurdly expensive and consequently prohibitory for the poor, the improvement that was made was that four gentlemen from the Private Bills Committee of this House were sent over to sit with the members of the Senate Divorce Committee so that they might personally hear the evidence which was given instead Of being compelled to read it after it was printed. I submit to this House that if we claim to be a legislative body, if we claini to be representative of the people of this country, it is hardly dealing fairly-I might almost say sincerely-with an important question such as this to give it such a remedy as the appointment of four more members to seats on a committee that, I imagine, practically every member of the House admits . never should have existed.
If we would consider the position we occupy as members of this House, it should not be very difficult to secure reform. We are very apt to speak of this member as being the member for this constituency and of that other member as being the member for that constituency, which is altogether contrary to the principle upon which we are elected to Parliament. I imagine there is no great difference of opinion as to the constitutional principle that theoretically every man in Canada has a part in the making of the laws, but
that, inasmuch as practically it is impossible for every man to come to Ottawa, the country is divided into districts in which the electors assemble to elect representatives of all the people of Canada. Each member who sits in this House to-day from the province of Quebec is just as truly a representative of the province of Ontario, Alberta, or British Columbia, as any member from any one of these provinces. It may be that the member selected by the electors in a certain constituency would be expected to be better aoquamted with the requirements of that constituency, but constitutionally, he is no more a representative of the people of that constituency than he is of any other people in any other constituency in Canada, for every member sitting in this House is the representative of all the people of Canada.
If that be the case, and the question is, I submit, beyond peradventure, and when it is shown that a grievance does exist, that some people in this country are put on a different footing from other people, is it not the duty of this House, and of each member of it, to see that whatever should be done is done in order to avoid such an unfortunate-I might almost say disastrous-result as having a line drawn, such as we have in the case of divorce, by which the rich in this country get divorces and the poor do not?
I well remembe! that in days gone by attempts have been made to remedy the law and that it has been found almost impossible. Many hon. members of .the House remember that for a long time in England there were a couple of hundred offences punishable with death. Philanthropists and legislators endeavoured, year after year, to secure some change in the law from Parliament, but their efforts were hopeless. In those days a man was hanged for stealing five shillings. It was impossible to obtain a change in the law until it happened that a servant stole a crown piece from the mantel; he was seen stealing it, he was arrested, brought before a judge and jury, the evidence given was conclusive and the jury was compelled to find that the coin had been stolen, but, unwilling to have the blood of that unfortunate man upon their heads, they said that they found him guilty of stealing a coin of the value of 4s. llid. The finding of that jury produced a change in the law of England.
It is a well-known fact that the law of divorce for many long years had been in a very unsatisfactory condition in England.

Attempt after attempt was made to change the law, but the result was very much as it is here. Divorce could only be obtained by Act of Parliament, but in order to obtain an Act of Parliament it was necessary to obtain a divorce in the ecclesiastical courts a mensa et thoro, then sue for damages, and then come to Parliament and obtain your Bill. It had been found impossible to persuade the legislature to take any steps to remedy this most ridiculous procedure until subsequent to 1845, when, in the case of Queen vs. Hall, Mr. Justice Maule gave his famous judgment. In that case a man was brought before Mr. Justice Maule charged with bigamy. The evidence was perfectly clear that the wife had run away with -another man, that she was then living with him, and that after this had continued for some time the prisoner had married again. The evidence being of this nature, the jury found the man guilty and Mr. Justice Maule proceeded to pass sentence. He told him first that he should have brought action for damages, that he should have then instituted a suit in the ecclesiastical courts for a divorce a mensa et thoro, and that he should then have obtained an act of Parliament dissolving his marriage. Then he told him that this would probably cost him a thousand pounds and that if he said he did not have that many pence it made no difference, because it was his duty to tell the prisoner that there was not one law for the rich and one for the poor, that as he had violated the law, he must be suitably punished, the punishment being imposed in these words:
You will be imprisoned for one day. And as you have now been in gaol since the commencement of the assizes, your term is more than expired; you are free.
This sentence brought the legislature in the Old Country to its senses and in consequence of that pronouncement by Mr. Justice Maule that absurd law was changed. We know that it is only a little over a century ago since legislatures were willing to have witches burned, and acts of that kind done, and we must not thinks that because laws are as they are they axe absolutely the best that can be made because changes have been made in such laws as these even within the last hundred years.
When we consider the position of Canada in regard to divorce, it seems to me that it does not require very much argument to induce the House to agree that something 
should be done. We are not the only civilized country in the world; we must admit, I suppose, that there are a few others. Yet, there are only two countries; in the world, claiming to be civilized,-which do not allow divorce-Italy and Spain. There is only one other country in which the divorce law is as it is in Canada and that is poof old Ireland. I can quite understand that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) will hardly argue that the laws in force in Ireland for the last hundred years are so absolutely perfect that you cannot improve them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They do not make the laws in Ireland; that is the trouble.

But I am sure the Minister of Justice will say that, if they were able to make laws in Ireland, they would make a more satisfactory and Christian law than they have there at the present time on this subject. There are only these two countries, Italy and Spain, in which they have no law of divorce. Let me briefly run through the list of civilized countries as given in the report of the Matrimonial Divorce - Commission (which sat in the Old Country for several years, presided over by Lord Gorrell) which have divorce courts. In Scotland divorce is granted not merely for adultery, but for desertion, and they have divorce courts in the following parts of the Empire: England, South Africa, Natal, New South Wales, New Zealand, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia, and India.
So there is not much doubt what the feeling of British subjects is with regard to this matter. Not only 'in the Motherland, but in every part of the Empire, divorces are obtained through the court.
Not in Newfoundland.

I was coming to that. Apparently, Newfoundland has no way of granting divorces, but I presume the same inherent right exists in their legislature as exists in ours, and that their legislature could grant a divorce. Divorces are granted by courts in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Roumania, Russia, Sweden, Switzerland, and in the United States. With only two exceptions then, it is an understood thing among the civilized nations of the world that divorces can be granted. It is only in Ireland that the same system of granting divorces exists as obtains here.

Up to 1857 there was no divorce court in England, and divorces were granted there the same as here, l?y Act of Parliament, but in that year a divorce court was established -a step far beyond anything we have in this country. In 1909 the warrant was issued to the Royal Commission on Divorce and Matrimonial Cases, and the House will pardon me if I read a couple of sentences [DOT]of the warrant:
We do hereby empower you to make an interim report with a view of enabling such steps as you may recommend to be taken for the redress of any hardship from which, in your opinion, the poorer classes may suffer under the existing law and administration.
The commission presented a minority and a majority report, but with the latter I have nothing to do, because it does not relate in any way to the motion before us to-day. I may say, however, that it recommends that the grounds upon which divorce is granted in England should be extended; to include, for instance, such cases as incurable insanity, imprisonment for life, and desertion, but I am not concerned with the majority report at all, for my motion does not seek to extend the grounds. 'The minority report, which is signed by the Primate of England (Cosmo Ebor), Sir William Anson, M.P., and Sir Lewis T. Dibbin, tvliile differing from the majority recommendation that the grounds be extended, went as far as I am asking this House to go; that
4 p.m. is, they recommend that steps should be taken in order to secure the possibility of divorces being *granted to the poor as well as to the rich. Let me read a few words from page 189 of the minority report:
We concur in the recommendation of your colleagues that local courts exercising the jurisdiction of the High Court should be established. We also agree that it will be convenient that these courts should be held at centres where there is already a'District Registry of the High Court.
These three gentlemen, then, are willing to have the facilities for divorce, which are so much greater in England than here, extended still further.
I should like to call attention to the fact that in my motion there is not one word about a court. I am merely pointing out that the present system is not satisfactory, and I ask the Government and this House either to contradict me and say that it is satisfactory, or to agree that it is unsatisfactory, and then like men rise to the occasion and try to reform our present system. When I brought this motion before the House a couple of years ago, war had not
broken out. I think the war has in many ways changed the position of many people in this country. I confess, Sir, I cannot understand how any one in this country can appeal to our young married men to fall in under the colours and fight for our country and Empire, and at the same time say	to them,	as	we arepractically	saying to	them to-day:If you are rich and happen to be wronged in your household while you are awaj, file your petition with the Senate, and the remedy will be provided. But if you are poor we can do nothing for you, because under our Canadian la"' a divorce cannot he granted except under these two conditions : first, the crime of the offending party, and second the wealth of the injured party. Only last week a most pitiful case appeared in the Toronto papers. It was that of a married man who had been among the first to enlist. While in Europe some scoundrel took advantage of his absence. Now, under our present law, we are compelled to say to that man:	We can do nothing for you;
if you lived in Montreal and were rich, we would have been quite prepared to grant a divorce, but as you live in Toronto and are poor there is no divorce for you in Canada. Does it not strike every member of this House as an injustice that makes his blood boil that we should ask these men to go to the front, and then crawl in behind them to protect ourselves at their expense, and then stand ready to give them a kick the moment the war is over. I appeal to this House whether that is the way to treat the men who are fighting for us, and are ready to give their lives for this country and the Empire. Let us either abolish divorce so that no man in Canada can have it, or adopt such procedure that the man who is fighting for his country, and risking his life for the Empire, has the same rights as his wealthier brothers.
If I may judge from the last debate on this subject in this House, there must havn been a misunderstanding of the history of the subject. As my hon. friend from Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) told us two years ago, we know that one great religious body, the Roman Catholic Church, is opposed to divorce. But nobody who knows anything about the subject would pretend to say that the Greek Church-another great branch of the Christian churches opposed to divorce. They have always had it, and have it to-day. The Anglican Church has never been opposed to divorce, and is not opposed to it to-day. Let me refer for a

moment to Volume 3 of the findings of the Royal Commission, page 441.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does the Greek Church grant divorce through, civil or ecclesiastical courts?

Through their consis-torial courts. On page 441 of the commission's report, Sir Edward Clarke, one of the best known counsel in England, in giving his evidence before the commission says that there is a popular misunderstanding on the subject of divorce, and he i quoted to show that even among the early Fathers of the Church there was a diversity of opinion. He referred to St. Augustine, St. Jerome and St. Ambrose,- none more famous-all of whom at one time had supported divorce and re-marriage. St. Augustine, it is true, changed his opinion later; but even he, toward the close of his life, declared that while his own opinion was against divorce, yet the subject was so uncertain that he would not blame any man who took a different view. Then Professor Denney, at page 264 of the same volume, quotes a number of. cases from the Fathers-
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr! Northrup) say that the Catholic Church does not recognize any divorce today?

It does not. The
Roman Catholic Church, ever since the Council of Trent in 1553, where it laid down the principle, has been absolutely against divorce and, does not recognize divorce.

I can tell my hon.
friend that he is wrong.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the Roman Catholic Church does recognize divorce?
For certain reasons.

Perhaps the hon.
gentleman refers to the case of marriage with a heathen?

No.
Mr. NORTHRUP. I believe the hon. gentleman is mistaken. Like a good many others he has misunderstood the case. The Roman Catholic Church does not recognize divorce. It does recognize divorce a mensa et thoro, separating the parties in a manner the counterpart of our English judicial separation, but with no right in either of the parties to r.e-marry.

I beg to contradict the
hon. gentleman again, for incompetency for instance, the Catholic Church does allow divorce and re-marriage.
I do not profess to-know more of the doctrines of the hon. gentleman's church than he knows himself,, but I think he is confusing nullification with divorce.
You go to the divorce courts to get it.

No. I have many authorities here, but as I do not wish to encumber Hansard with a number of theological opinions, I will merely give the pages of the report in order that those who wish to do so may read for themselves. At page 264 of Volume III of these reports, Professor Denney gives a list, quoting in one case Gregory II, who was in favour of divorce. At page 437 of the same volume, Sir Frederick Pollock, professor of law in Oxford University, recognized as one of the ablest writers on English law who ever lived, gives a list of authorities of the Fathers of the early days, who, he says, were in favour of divorce. The evidence before the committee was to the effect that in England there had never been a time when it was thfi law of the land, or even the final law of the church, that divorce-could not be given. Away back in A.D. 686, Archbishop Theodore had a canon passed, a copy of which I' have before me, in which he expressed himself as opposed to divorce and re-marriage; but the same archbishop, in his Penitentials, which he put in the hands of his clergy, .authorized them, though counselling their parishioners to abstain from divorce and re-marriage, yet to allow them, if they insisted, to marry again.
My hon. friend (Mr. Carroll) has spoken about certain grounds on which the Roman Catholic Church does give divorce. As he has brought the matter up, I may be allowed to refer to it without incurring the charge of making an attack upon that Church. I would refer to the evidence of Mgr. Moyes, who attended this commission, as representative of the Archbishop of Westminster, for the purpose of stating what was the doctrine of the Roman Catholic Church on this subject. I cannot be accused of attacking the Church if I read what he gave as being the doctrine of the Church:
The inpediments which are held by the Catholic church -to be diriment or nullifying are the following:	1. Error, as to person. 2.

Condition (if A marries B, a slave, believing B to be free). 3. Solemn vow of chastity or entering religious order, made before consummation of marriage. 4. Consanguinity to third degree. 5. Crime (if A during a former marriage with B has committed adultery with C, with promise of marriage after death of B, and if A or C has attempted the life of B, the marriage of A and C is null). 6. Disparity of worship, viz:	marriage of a Christian with a
non-Christian. 7. Duress or violence affecting liberty of consort. 8. Holy order to which is attached obligation of chastity. 9. The bond of preceding marriage (if either party have a husband or wife still alive). 10. Public decorum (if one of the parties is solemnly or publicly betrothed to another person.) 11. Madness or amentia (viz, imbecility, precluding reasonable consent). 12. Affinity. 13. Clandestinity. 14. Impotency. 15. Rape.
So, the grounds he gives are those for nullification; not for a divorce a vinculo in our sense, with rights of the parties to re-marry. I am not finding fault with these rules of the Roman Catholic Church. There are many cases in which marriages were nullified by the church. There is one case so well known that every member of ' the House may be acquainted with it. There was a girl in England named Margaret Tudor, of very respectable family. Her father was Henry Tudor, better known as Henry VII, and her brother is more widely though less favourably known in history as Henry VIII. She married a Scotchman, known as James Stuart, afterwards James IV of Scotland. She was the sister-in-law of Louis XII of France, and so the double grandmother of Mary Queen of Soots, the direct descendant of Whom sits on the throne of Great Britain to-day. So, you see, when we speak of Margaret Tudor, we are dealing with a very respectable family. When Margaret Tudor lost her husband James, she married- that is she went through the marriage ceremony with-the Earl of Angus. Some time later, being weary of Angus, she discovered that, while he had never been married before, he had had a betrothal to the daughter of the Earl of Bothwell. So, there was a nullification of that marriage. Then, she married Lord Methven. But, wearying of him, and there being no divorce, she discovered that he was related in the fourth degree to the Earf of Angus, and so her marriage to Lord Methven was nullified. Some people might have thought that as it had been decided that she had never been married to the Earl of Angus, the law declaring that his relationship with Lord Methven was a bar to her marriage with Methven was not sound. Still, that was the law as adjudged and as administered. So that when my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll)
speaks about divorce he should remember that it is not divorce that is given, but absolute nullification of marriage. I can quite Understand that a gentleman belonging to the church of my hon. friend would have this objection to divorce, which, perhaps, is not well founded. The people affected by the nullification of marriage as it was practised in Europe for many centuries were not the lower classes or the poor-those for whom I am pleading today. At that time only the rich or the mighty were concerned either in divorce or in the nullification of marriage. Divorce, if provision had been made for it in those days, could have been comparatively simple and comparatively inexpensive; but those who desired to set aside the marriage tie-persons of nobility or crowned heads-could well afford to pay. If the grounds of application, therefore, were abstruse and difficult to prove, there would, to the ecclesiastical lawyers, be an advantage in nullification rather than in divorce. Take the case of a man who desired to be free from the marriage tie and wished to marry some one else. If he obtained a divorce, one day the eldest son would take his title or his crown, as the case might be, with all [DOT] his estates; but if he stepped out free and unencumbered, he could offer to the lady of his heart for the time being all that he had to give-title, estate, position foi^ her life and for her son after her. In the light of these facts, some people may be inclined to attach to divorce some objections that are not properly attachable' to it, but that were properly attachable to nullification. In England or in any country where divorces are granted, the children of divorced persons are protected; they go forth as free as if the marriage had not been set aside at all, with their birthright preserved.
When the hon. member for Rouville was speaking on this subject two years ago, he called attention to the fact that in the Republic to the south of us there had been a great multiplication of divorces; that there was actually one divorce to every twelve marriages. My hon. friend mentioned this as an objection to the resolution I then had before the House. But I am afraid my hon. friend's figures were such as to lead to a wrong conclusion. Apart from census statistics, what a shocking state of affairs it would be if there was one divorce to every twelve marriages in Ottawa! Similarly, I am sure our friends to the south would
There have been cases where the fees have been remitted, have there not?

You can sue in forma
pauperis, and, if you do, certain disbursements in the Senate are forgiven; but you have to do your advertising, to serve the . respondent, to employ counsel, and to bring witnesses here. Suppose we take the extreme case of people from Alberta or Saskatchewan; apart from everything else, what would be the expense of bringing witness from one of those provinces to Ottawa?
I have been very careful not to advocate a court. I have been trying all the way through to confine myself to suggestions that are practicable with our existing system. 1 quite understand that if I said a word about a court different objections would be raised; but I can see ways in which a tremendous improvement could be made in the present procedure, a wonderful saving, even using the imperfect machinery we have. Therefore, I have been very careful not to suggest a court, although one cannot help seeing that to make our procedure conform with that of other civilized lands it would be necessary to have a court. But if we Canadians cannot rise to the plane of other peoples, if we do not possess the intelligence, if we do not possess the hearts of other peoples, let us at least do the best we can, and so arrange our divorce laws that as many as possible who are entitled to can avail themselves of the law. Let us not have it confined only to the few.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Has the hon. member made any estimate or can he submit any figures as to the actual difference in cost to a petitioner who applies for and obtains a divorce through Parliament, and a peti-



tioner who applies for and obtains a divorce through one of the courts, say in British Columbia, New Brunswick or Nova Scotia.
That is perfectly correct.
It is perfectly true you might have a case in British Columbia in which you would have to bring witnesses from England.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It would largely depend on where the witnesses come from.

Supposing you had a court like the judge of the Exchequer Court, who goes to Alberta, or Manitoba, or Saskatchewan, at certain times and holds court there. There is no one in Saskatchewan or Alberta so poor that lie or she could not bring witnesses to that place. But it is a different thing to employ counsel there, to have that counsel employ counsel in Ottawa, to pay the expenses of advertising and the expenses of service, to bring your witnesses to Ottawa -and then on coming here perhaps find that the Senate had adjourned for the week and that you would have to keep the witnesses waiting to be heard. It makes all the difference whether you have one procedure or the other. As my hon. friend suggests the courts, let me recite to the House a case told me by one of the leading lawyers in British Columbia, formerly a member of this House. A lady from Ontario married a gentleman who was the manager of a bank in British Columbia. Her father was a wealthy man. The boom in real estate struck British Columbia. The bank manager was carried away by it and went deeply into it. He sent for his father-in-law, who went out to British Columbia, and then the bank manager inveigled the father-in-law into real estate. They went in deeper and deeper until one fine day the son-in-law disappeared and the father-in-law found he was a ruined man. The wife was left with three children and not a penny. She who had never supported herself in her life had to go out and support herself and her three small children, and she did it with difficulty. My informant, on hearing the story, was very much affected by it and desired to do what he could. On think-
	; ;
ing it over he" said: I believe that man who came from England probably went back. He employed a detective in London and found he was living in his own village in England very comfortably with a lady, supposedly his wife, who was introduced and recognized as his wife. At once my friend told the deserted wife:	I will get
you a divorce, and he was prepared to get it. But it happens that the law of British Columbia is the law of England which was in force at the time the court was established in British Columbia, and the law of England at that time was that while a husband could obtain a divorce for adultery, the wife was obliged to show adultery plus cruelty. Since then the law has been changed in England, so that now desertion for two years is taken as cruelty. But the British Columbia law is the old English law, and although this lady was entitled to apply to the court and could show that her husband was living in the Old Country with another, woman, she could not prove cruelty, and therefore could not get a divorce in British Columbia. I said to the gentleman:	Why do you not come to
Ottawa? He said:	Why didn't I? I was
willing to put the case through for her at my own expense; I was willing to put up $500 or $1,000; but when I considered that it meant employing detectives in the Old Country, bringing them out here to give evidence, as there is no means of taking evidence under commission under our divorce proceedings, keeping them here for Heaven knows how long, and that it might then turn out that I would have to send somebody from here over there to identify the man there as being really the husband of the lady, the probable expense was so tremendous that I was obliged to abstain altogether. That is just an illustration of how, even where you have a court, if your laws are not satisfactory you may have hard cases. But if you have such a hard case as that where there is a court, as in British Columbia, it is not difficult to understand that there will be exceedingly hard cases under such circumstances as we have here.
There are a good many other things I intended to say and would have liked to say, but I feel I am trespassing on the indulgence of the House. Let me, in conclusion, merely repeat the points I would like to impress on the House-and I hope that nobody will answer what I have said to-day by presenting arguments against an extension of the grounds on which divorce

is granted, for I have not touched that at all. I hope that every member of this House will appreciate his position. Every man in this House is a representative of everybody in this country and is responsible for seeing that justice is done to everybody in this country. While I quite understand and appreciate the position of a member of a great church which is opposed to divorce who, when divorce Bills are brought before this House, does not vote on them, I think I, as a member of another faith, might well appeal to him and say:	In this case, inasmuch as you and
others of your church do not ask for divorces, as you are not affected by these divorces, it will in no way hurt you' to support the changes I propose, if you find that in every civilized land but two outside of Canada there is a simpler way of obtaining divorces. If we desire to treat the poor as we treat the rich, we must do one of two things. Take the cases I mentioned where two men went across the sea, one from Montreal and one from Toronto, both apparently entitled to apply to Parliament for divorces if one can believe the papers, and one can apply because he has money and the other cannot apply because he has not, although the facts are there, his home is broken up, a little one not his is there to meet him on his, return. It seems to me that any man who has one single drop of red blood in his veins must feel that, whatever we do, whether or not we can decide upon a complete remedy for these evils, we should at least be men enough to do the best we can, so that if only in such cases as the half dozen poor women to whom I referred a moment ago, we relieve them of the burden which is such a load upon them to-day, we could say that we had done something this session of which we would have reason to be proud until our dying day.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with very great interest indeed to the masterly address delivered by my hon. friend the member for East Hastings. Let me at once commend his ability, his fairness, and his broadmindedness. I say his broad-mindedness, because in the course of his speech he seemed to fear that has remarks might be taken as adverse to one church. Let me say to the hon. gentleman that he would be the last of all men in this House to use any arguments which could be taken as adverse to any of the great churches of this country. He is well known for his fairness,
49i
and he has approached the subject on this occasion, as he did on the last in a fair and broad-minded spirit. I may also tell him that it is not from a sectarian point of view that I rise to oppose his motion; I speak as a Canadian having in view the welfare of our country, and I shall try to demonstrate in as few words as possible that the position I take is in the best interests of Canada. I shall try to demonstrate in a few moments that though my hon. friend's motion apparently affects only the * procedure of divorce, it would tend to create a substantive law of divorce in provinces where it does not exist at present. I repeat that I approach this question from a national point of view.
It so happens that the Catholic Church is not the only church opposed to divorce. In the course of his very able remarks, my hon. friend said that the Anglican Church was not opposed to divorce. I do not know the tenets of the Anglican Church in England, but I know that the Anglican Church oi Canada is just as much opposed to divorce, as the Roman Catholic Church is. On the last occasion, when I spoke on this question, I quoted a canon which had been unanimously adopted on the question of marriage and divorce at the sessions of the Anglican Synod, held in Montreal in 1905. That canon read as follows:
No clergyman within the jurisdiction of the Church of England in Canada shall solemnize a marriage between persons either of whom shall have been divorced from one who is living at the time.
So, I biush aside any sectarian point of view. I do not wish to be dogmatic in the matter; I am speaking as a Canadian, feeling that if this Parliament should in any way whatsoever facilitate the procedure of divorce such a change would tend *to create a much larger number of divorces before our courts and before this Parliament, and would be detrimental to the best interests of our common country. My view, therefore, is that we should not increase the facilities for obtaining divorce, which have been criticised by my hon. friend, but that, on the contrary-and this is where I join issue with him-we should restrict these facilities, or at least we should leave the procedure as it is, and as it was intended to be at the time our Divorce Committee was organized after Confederation.
The question is not new. The hon. member has brought it before the House on several occasions, the last time being in 1914, I think, but I doubt whether; since that time, in spite of the very able address

of my hon. friend, there has been any demand in the country for the legislation which he is urging by his motion this afternoon. His address will be read with great interest from the historical point of view, as well as from the legal point of view. In fact, I am surprised that such an able gentleman as my hon. friend from Hastings does not adorn the benches of the Government, or the bench of the high courts of Ontario. Since his address in this House in 1914, I believe he has addressed two public institutions in this country, the Canadian Club and the Forum, but there has been no serious demand for the legislation which he urges *this Parliament to enact. It is a very vexed question. By many people, possibly by the majority in this House, marriage is considered as only a civil contract, but to many others, certainly to a respectable minority in this country, embracing all races and all creeds, marriage is more than a civil contract; it is also a sacrament. Therefore Parliament should be careful about opening the gates to any legislation affecting marriage, the effect of which would be to assail and endanger the very foundations of Canadian society. In four provinces they have divorce courts, and as my hon. friend has stated, five others have no divorce courts. When the subject came up before Parliament in 1914, the question of our jurisdiction in this Dominion Parliament was well put by the Minister of Justice. He gave us the meaning and the extent of the power vested in the Dominion Parliament. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, let me read the very weighty words of the Minister of Justice, who we all know has, for many years, with conspicuous ability, sat on the bench, and who is a very eminent jurist. Speaking in the course of that debate, the Minister of Justice thus defined the powers of Parliament on this question. He said:
I understand perfectly that In those provinces-
That is to say, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia

-which have divorce courts and which have also a. substantive law which those courts can administer and supply, prescribing the causes giving the right to divorce, the principle of divorce is recognized by the law. But in the five provinces where those conditions do not exist, not only the oourts have not jurisdiction to pronounce divorces but there is no law under which anybody is entitled to a divorce; and if this Parliament confined itself to giving jurisdiction to hear divorce cases to courts in

those provinces, those oourts would sit with no law to apply. You cannot, to any purpose, confide to the court the procedure-to use the word of the motion-by which divorces are to be obtained, until you have first made a substantive law to which that procedure is going to apply.
In other words, my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup), able as he is, has begun his agitation at the wrong end. He is agitating for a more pliable procedure. He *should begin by advocating in these five provinces the enactment of substantive laws on divorce. He might have a pliable procedure, but he would have no law to apply the procedure to. To go on with the remarks by the Minister of Justice on that occasion:
This Parliament, to use the expression of the hon. member, grants divorce on a particular ground, passes one Act for one individual, and why does it do it? Because that individual has come to it and said: I want to be an exception to the general law. We talk about coming to Parliament to obtain divorces and we talk about the procedure by which divorces are granted but the whole operation is a legislative Act, and when a man comes to Parliament, on the face of his application he does not ask for a Bill to divorce anybody, but he asks for an Act for the relief of so and so; and relief from what? Prom an obligation that the general law imposes upon him. In those provinces where there is no divorce court their is equally no divorce law, and the general law of those provinces, I have no hesitation in saying, does not know divorce. Most assuredly in the province I come from the law does not know divorce, and it is because there is no law in force that persons, seeking it require special legislation. Bet me speak of my own province-although I have no doubt I shall be borne out by lawyers from the other provinces *-the man who comes here, say from the province of Quebec, and asks this Parliament for a divorce, is asking to be made an exception to the law. He comes here because, by law, he has no right to a divorce. If by law he had a right to a divorce, it would naturally follow that that would be a right enforceable in a court. The reason why-people have to come here is not because the courts have not jurisdiction ; it is because there is no law which the courts could administer if they had the amplest jurisdiction.
In these words the Minister of Justice has gone to the very crux of the question. This Parliament grants relief to so and so from living according to the general law in the province where he comes from; this Parliament does not grant divorce to so and so.
.My hon. friend does not seem to attach much importance to statistics. First of all, let me tell him that the statistics which I used two years ago were taken from an address delivered by a very eminent member of the United States Congress. On that occasion I had applied to the Parlia-

mentary Library to get a special report which had been prepared by Mr. Carroll Wright in 1906. Unfortunately, that report was not on the Shelves at that time, so I had to rely on what this address of the United States senator contained. I will, however, in a few moments, give the House the statistics from the official source. My hon. friend himself will be obliged to agree with me in saying that these statistics are simply appalling, and he will be obliged to say with me that divorce, as an institution in the United States, with the facilities which have been granted by the various legislatures of the Commonwealth, has become the greatest curse of the American Republic. But first of all, let me, Mr. Speaker, give the figures which affect our own case in Canada. As the result of a motion I made the other day, I obtained the following figures with regard to divorces granted by the Parliament of Canada from 1867 to 1915 inclusive. The total number granted was 285-to husbands 158, and to wives 127. By provinces the figures are as follows: Ontario 175, Quebec 42, Manitoba 25, Saskatchewan 8, Alberta 15, British Columbia 2, Northwest Territories 7, Prince Edward Island 1. So that, on the whole, although the number of divorces has been increasing of late, we may fairly claim that in Canada we have a clean sheet compared with that of other countries. But I repeat that if we should facilitate the procedure in the way advocated by my good friend from Hastings, it would tend, in my humble judgment, to make the matrimonial tie lax instead of binding. I say again that the statistics published by the United States Government are simply appalling, and that the example of the United States should be a warning to the Canadian legislator. There are many institutions in the United States which we admire and would willingly borrow, but I regret to say that the divorce statistics published by the United States should be a warning and a lesson to us. By virtue of an Act passed by Congress, two investigations have been held in the United States on the question of divorce. The first investigation covered the period from 1867 to 1886, and the second from 1887 to 1906; that is, each investigation covered a period of twenty years. Of. course, one cannot draw up a bill of indictment against any one nation in particular, or against a whole people. I think my hon. friend in the course of his speech admitted the gravity of this question in the United States, and in this connection I should like to quote the words of a well known
ex-President of the Republic-a man whose name is highly respected in his own country and abroad. I refer to ex-President Roosevelt. As a result of petitions presented to Congress, that the
5 p.m. matter was of sufficient importance to warrant another investigation, President Roosevelt sent a special message to Congress creating a new commission. Before the commission set to work, he addressed its members in the following language:
Bishop Doane and gentlemen:
It is a very great pleasure to meet you here. There is a certain tendency to exalt the unessential in dealing with our public questions, and public men especially are apt to get their attention concentrated on questions that have an importance, but a wholly ephemeral importance, compared with the questions that go straight to the root of things. Questions like the tariff and the currency are of literally no consequence whatsoever compared with the vital question of having the unit of our social life, the home, preserved. It is impossible to overstate the importance of the cause you represent. If the average husband and wife fulfil their duties toward one another and toward their children as Christianity teaches them, then we may rest absolutely assured that the other problems will solve themselves. But if we have solved every other problem in the wisest possible way it shall profit us nothing if we have lost our own national soul, and we will have lost it if we do not have the question of the relations of the family put upon the proper basis.
I should like to call the attention of my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup.) to the sentence which follows. My hon. friend admitted that the matrimonial tie might be lax in the United States, but he suggested that that was only in the southern portion, amongst coloured people. President Roosevelt says :
One of the most unpleasant and dangerous features of our American life is the diminishing birth rate, the loosening of the marital tie among the old native American families. It goes without saying that, for the race as for the individual, no material prosperity, no business growth, no artistic or scientific development will count if the race commits suicide. Therefore, Bishop, I count myself fortunate in having the chance to work with you in this matter of vital importance to the national welfare.
From the report of that commission, which President Roosevelt addressed in these ominous words, I have collated some statistics, and to me they are simply appalling. Sir, it is terrible to think that such a great and noble democracy as the neighbouring republic to the south has fallen to such a level in one of the most vital problems of its national life. The growth of divorce in the United States

under the general divorce laws has been unprecedented, and the divorce figures exceed in number those of any other modern nation excepting Japan. Ah analysis of the statistics prepared by Carroll D. Wright, Commissioner of Labour, in 1S89, showed the total number of divorces for a period of twenty years, from 1867 to 1887, to be 328,716, an increase of 157 per cent, while the increase in population for the same period was 60 per cent. The Census Bulletin upon marriage and divorce in the United States, issued by the Department of Labour and Commerce under authority of an Act of Congress, in 1908, shows that the total number of divorces for the entire country from 1887 to 1906 inclusive was 945,625. For the earlier investigation covering tjie twenty years from 1867 to 1886 inclusive, the number reported was 328,716, or hardly more than one-third of the number reported in the second twenty years.
At the beginning of the forty-year period covered by the two investigations, divorces occurred at the rate of 10,000 a year. At the end of that period the annual number was about 66,000. This increase, however, must be considered in connection with the increase in population. An increase of 30 per cent in population between the years 1870 and 1880, was accompanied by an increase of 79 per cent in the number of divorces granted. In the next decade, 1880 to 1890, the population increased 25 per cent and divorces 70 per cent. In the following decade, 1890 to 1900, an increase of 21 per cent in population was accompanied by an increase of 66 per cent in the number of divorces. In the next six years, from 1900 to 1906, population, as estimated, increased 10-5 per cent, and divorces 29-3 per cent. It thus appears that at the end of the forty-year period divorces were increasing about three times as fast as the population, while in the first decade, 1870 to 1880, they increased only about two and two-thirds as fast.
The divorce rate per 100,000 population increased from 29 in 1870 to 82 in 1905. In the former year there was one divorce for every 3,441 persons and in the latter year one for every 1,218. The rate per 100,000 married population was 81 in the year 1870 and 200 in the year 1900. This comparison indicates that divorce is at present two and one-half times as common, compared with married population, as it was forty years ago. Divorce rates appear to be much higher in the United States than in any of the foreign countries for which statistics relating to this subject have been obtained. Two-thirds of the total number
of divorces granted in the twenty-year period covered by this investigation were granted to the wife.
The most common single ground for divorce is desertion. This accounts for 38-9 per cent of all divorces granted in the period 1887 to 1906, 49-4 per cent or almost one-half those granted to the husband, and 33-5 per cent or one-third of those granted to the wife. The next most important ground of divorce is, for husbands, adultery, and for wives, cruelty. Of the divorces granted to husbands in the period from 1887 to 1906, 28'8 per cent were for adultery, and of those granted to wives 27,5 per cent were for cruelty. Only 10 per cent of the divorces granted to wives were for adultery of the husband, and 10-5 per cent of divorces granted to husbands were for cruelty on the part of the wife. Drunkenness was the ground for divorce, in 5-3 per cent of the cases for which the wife brought suit, and in 1-4 per cent of the cases in which the suit was brought by the husband. Intemperance was reported as an indirect or contributory cause for divorce in 5 per cent of the divorces granted to the husband, and in 18 per cent of the divorces granted to the wife, and appeared as a direct or indirect cause in 19-5 per cent of all divorces, and 26-3 per cent of those granted to wives, and 6-1 per cent of those granted to husbands. Only 15 per cent of the divorces were returned as contested and probably in many of these cases the contesting was haTdly more than a formality.
The average duration of marriages terminated by divorce is about ten years. Sixty per cent, or three-fifths, last less than ten years, and 40 per cent last longer. Of the divorced couples known to have been married in the United States, 88.5 per cent were married in the same state in -which they were divorced. Of all the divorced couples known to have been married in foreign countries, 36-9 per cent were married in Canada, 12-7 per cent in England, 16-1 per cent in Germany, and 1-9 per cent in Ireland. Children were reported in 39-8 per cent of the total number of divorced cases. The proportion is much larger for divorces granted to the wife than for divorces granted to the husband; children being present in 46,8 per cent of the former class of divorces and 26 per cent of the latter. A reason suggested for this is that the children are usually assigned by the court to- the mothers, and to her, therefore, divorce does not imply separation from her

children, while to the husband it involves a severance of the parental as well as the marital relation.
In England there were 284 divorces in 1902, as compared with 177 in 1901. In Germany, at the same time, there were about 10,000, annually, and in France 21,939, with a tendency towards a rapid increase. Among the Japanese there are about 100,000 divorces per annum. It is estimated that about fifty per cent of divorced couples have children, and it is urged "that consideration for the children of divorced people should be a first concern in stimulating restrictive legislation." It has been stated that three-quarters of the boys in two reformatories, one in Ohio and one in Illinois, come from families broken up by death or divorce, "mainly by divorce."
Now, these are the statistics that I have collected; I trust I have not wearied the House in reading them. I would ask any faix'-minded member of this House if such a statement as I have given is not most significant. Are not these statistics the most palpable evidence that there is, to use the classical expression, "something rotten in the state of Denmark"? Sir, we are engaged in building up to the best of our ability this young country of ours. Canada takes her ideals from Great Britain, from France, from the United States. Is it not our duty to see to it that the moral foundations of our young country be made secure? And how can we make these foundations secure, nay, eternal, if not by first preserving the home and the sanctity of marriage?
Notwithstanding what has been said by some hon. members, I am optimistic as to the conditions that will face this country after the war. I believe that we shall receive millions of immigrants from the various countries of the world. We shall receive many from the Western States of America; we shall receive, and will welcome, many from the British Islands. Many will come from other parts of Europe, and I regret to say that among these will he some from those countries, enumerated by my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup), where divorce procedure is facilitated.
I freely grant that we can profit largely by the experiences of the countries of origin of our coming immigrants; permit me to say that we may benefit also by the gross errors of those countries. The compiler of this bulletin says, speaking of the United States:
Apparently the divorce rate, like the velocity of a falling body, is constantly increasing, and it is impossible to determine statistically from available data just what the results would be if the rate reached at any particular time remained constant. In other words, no statistics bearing on this question of the duration of marriages terminated by divorce have been obtained that accurately represent present conditions or conditions at any particular period; for the conditions are not static, but dynamic.
If the velocity of the divorce race is constantly increasing in the United States, I say it is our duty as Canadian legislators not to imitate the legislation under which the immigrants coming to our country from the United States have lived; it is our duty not to provide that these immigrants shall find in Canada statutory provisions in this respect similar to those in force in the Western States. If ever the adage " let well enough alone " was true, it is in regard to this matter. If you facilitate the procedure-and the motion of my hon. friend aims to facilitate it-you facilitate the causes. I say again that the greater facilities for divorce, the larger the number of divorces; more homes will be broken up, and the continuity of parental authority will be shattered. The welfare of the nation depends on the home; if you loosen the home ties, the welfare of the nation will be enormously affected.
The civil law of some provinces allows divorce a vinculo, as was stated by my hon. friend. The church law, on the contrary-when I say " church law I do not refer to the law uf one particular church, it is the law of the Anglican Church as well-allows divorce a mensa et thoro, which is the old term for separation. As I stated a moment ago, I do not wish to be dogmatic in this matter, but I say that I prefer the law of the church, whether it be the Roman Catholic Church or the Anglican Church; whether it be the law extolled by the best minds in the Protestant as well as in the Catholic world; I accept the view which condemns divorce as a violation of natural law. Husband and wife are parents of the same child, and the natural relationship of each to the child inevitably produces, as between husband and wife, a natural relationship one to the other. No decree of a court or no Act of Parliament can undo that relationship. If marriage is temporary and ephemeral, parentship is temporary and ephemeral. If the child is educated to regard parentship as a thing which can be set aside with the help of certain legal formalities, the whole structure on which our society rests will be undermined; if we

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I am one of those
who believe that divorce as administered in the United States has been a great curse to both the domestic and social life of that country, i I have 'been very much impressed by the speech just delivered by my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). Whether I act from conscientious scruples or from the views which my church takes on divorce, whether I am against divorce or not, we meet with the condition in this country that divorce is granted, and so I, under our civil laws, come to the same conclusion as my hon. friend from Hastings: that some reform is necessary in this country in the manner of divorce procedure. I do not, however, reach that conclusion on the same premises or on the same grounds as does my hon. friend.
I reach that conclusion not because the present facilities for obtaining divorce in this country are cumbersome, nor because they are expensive; I reach that conclusion, and in this I agree with my hon. friend from Hastings, because the procedure towards obtaining divorce is absurd. My hon. friend from Hastings has pictured the facility with which rich men in this country can obtain divorce, as compared with the outlawing, so to speak, of the poor man or poor woman who has proper grounds for obtaining divorce, but who has not the money. Of course, we meet with these conditions in every walk of life; we meet with them in our courts. How often do we meet persons in this country who have good cases to take before the courts and who could legally establish their rights, but who have not the money to fee counsel to argue their cases in the courts. From that point of view, I do not think that my
hon. friend from Hastings has made a very strong case.
But, Sir, let us look for a moment at the methods by which divorces are obtained- apart from the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and British Columbia, in the provinces whose inhabitants must come to this Parliament to obtain divorce. They go to the Senate; they make application by advertising in the Royal Gazette for six months, which is absurd; a Bill is introduced in the Senate, it is referred to a small Committee of the Senate which takes the evidence. I am not finding fault with the ability of the members of the Senate Committee to deal with any cause, and, I may say that, in my opinion, the chairman of that committee is one of the very ablest lawyers in Canada; a man well qualified to judge of what is, and what is not evidence. This small Committee of the Senate hears the evidence, passes it up to the Senate, and the evidence is printed. The Senate passes upon it, and then the evidence comes here. How many hon. members of this House ever take the trouble to yead that evidence, to see whether or not, in their estimation, as lawyers, or as citizens not of that avocation, the evidence is sufficient to justify the granting of divorce?
I say the proceeding is absurd. We vote on divorces in this House without knowing what we are voting on, and I believe that apart from the Senate Committee which hears the evidence, the Upper House is in the same position as we are.
I may point out that in the session of 1912 I took the trouble to read over the evidence in a divorce case which came from the Senate. I am a lawyer, and know something about the rules of evidence; I can distinguish fairly well what is and what is not evidence, and I came to the conclusion that, on the understanding that there was only one reason for which this Parliament can grant divorce, there was absolutely no evidence in that case which would entitle the applicant to divorce. I took the matter up in Committee of the Whole, and I got such support from the other members of this House that the Bill was thrown out. One would think that the counsel who had charge of that case, and who was paid for looking after it in the Senate would have undertaken to get all the evidence necessary to prove his case before the Senate Committee, but in the opinion of this House he did not do so. The following year he came back with an overwhelming

abundance of evidence; the application was not opposed, and I am given to understand that there was a mutual understanding between the parties that there should be no effort to oppose the divorce. That is only one instance, and I believe that Bills of divorce, or of relief, or whatever you care to call them, pass through this Parliament, and are granted by this Parliament every session where there is no evidence to support. That is the reason I agree with my hon. friend from Hastings that there should be some reform.
I believe, Sir, that this Parliament is not a proper tribunal to try divorce cases, for the reason that only a very small proportion of the members of this Parliament comes face to face, or in direct communication with the persons who seek divorce, and give their evidence. I take the ground that a judge who hears the evidence is the person qualified to grant the application or not as he deems fit. I take the stand that only one tribunal in this country is capable-I will use the word capable-of hearing and passing upon divorce cases, and that tribunal is to be found in our courts. I believe that in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick we have the very best tribunals in Canada for hearing and trying divorce cases. This Parliament is composed of men of different walks of life, it is composed, it is true, of some lawyers, and it is no reflection on the other members of the House, or of Parliament, to say that a lawyer is trained to understand what is evidence, and that the other members of Parliament are not so trained. While they have other merits far superior to those possessed by the lawyers in this Chamber or in the Senate, they have not the merit which enables them to pass upon such matters. In the province of Nova Scotia we have a divorce court, and it does not, as my hon. friend from Rouville seemed to think, if I understood him rightly, furnish a greater facility for obtaining divorce than doe3 this Parliament. I think, perhaps, it has the contrary effect, because I believe there are divorces granted by this Parliament which no judge in the country would grant if the cases came before him. So I say that, if this Parliament did undertake to reform the procedure of divorce, by handing over to the courts of Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the jurisdiction for granting divorce, it would not be giving easier facilities for obtaining divorce, but it would be safe__
gg?;: - -
guarding the marriage tie in this country to a very great extent indeed. That is my personal view. While, from conscientious scruples I am opposed to divorce, we have a condition in this country to deal with, and to meet that condition we should hand over the jurisdiction of trying divorce cases to the tribunals which are competent to handle them. I am not going to develop this argument any further, but I do say that I disagree with my hon. friend from Rouville when he says that the effect of reform in the way of giving jurisdiction to the courts would be to create easier facilities for obtaining divorce. My hon. friend from Rouville says that it might enlarge the grounds on which divorce is granted, but I do not understand the motion of the hon. member for Hastings to contemplate any such enlargement; I do not understand him to ask that other grounds for divorce should be added.
I do not so understand it and I listened to him very carefully. So, I think this House will be well advised, if it does take into consideration the motion of my hon. friend from East Hastings, if it does take away jurisdiction from this Parliament to hear evidence and pass upon divorce, and if it hands that jurisdiction over to the courts of those provinces which at present have not that jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty, as the representative of a constituency in Quebec, to declare that it is -creditable that every Roman Catholic member and senator since Confederation has had to vote, on principle, against divorce. No divorce Bill has ever passed this House, or the Senate, except "on division," and when I had the honour of occupying your Chair, Mr. Speaker, it was always my duty to declare that a divorce Bill passed "on division." Fifty members of this House are therefore debarred from voting on the merits of any of these petitions for divorce coming before it, and we are often asked not to oppose a divorce, or not to go to the committee, and allow a petition to go through. Therefore, one-quarter of this Parliament is debarred from dealing with this question at all.
I do not want to enter into the merits of this question of divorce. I am opposed to divorce on principle. I think that, far from extending the facilities for granting divorces, we should do everything to keep the divorce evil out of Canada. At Confederation, if divorce was recognized at all by the Dominion Parliament, it was prob-

ably because divorce courts were then in existence in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. They were not then in existence in Ontario, and they never will be in Quebec. But, whether they shall continue to exist or not, here or there, why we should grant greater facilities is something I cannot understand. There is no practical need of keeping up the custom of granting divorces. As far as Quebec is concerned, I do not believe any man or woman of my faith has ever applied to the Dominion Parliament for a divorce. The Roman Catholic church would not sanction it, and any person making application would be beyond the pale of the church.
I remember the late member for Niagara (Mr. Lancaster), an Anglican, making a very forcible speech in this House against divorce. Divorce appears to be one of the greatest curses in the United States to-day. Cardinal Gibbons, and a great many of the leading men in the United States, have declared against divorce. The fact that the principle has extended throughout the world is no argument in its favour. If Italy and Spain have been able to debar divorce it is to their credit. If you attack the home, you weaken the family tie, and you undermine the foundation of the state. The one great basic institution in this country is the home, and once the home is destroyed the state is of little account. I have heard distinguished lawyers in this House say that divorces have been granted on evidence on which a cat would not be hanged, and the way in which some divorce cases which I do not care to mention-have been dealt with, and are dealt with year after year, is almost a parody on justice. If the courts were to try causes as this Parliament has handled divorce cases, it would be nothing more nor less than a parody on justice. I have never given a vote for divorce, and I hope, so long as I am a member of this House, that I will do all I can to make divorce as difficult as possible to obtain. I believe that in so doing I am fulfilling the most sacred duty that a representative of the people has imposed upon him, and that is to do what he can to protect the home against an encroachment of this kind.
Mr. A. A. McLiEAN ("Queens, P.E.I.): Mr. Speaker, the statement has been made in the House that Prince Edward Island has a divorce court. We have a statute in Prince Edward Island which provides that any person who wants a divorce must petition the Lieutenant-Governor. The
expression " lieutenant-governor has been interpreted to mean the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, but the Lieutenant-Governor in Council has never authorized a court to hear divorce cases. As far as I know there has never been a divorce granted in Prince Edward Island, although the statute there provides that the lieutenant-governor may grant a fiat to the chief justice of the Supreme Court to try a divorce case. The lieutenant-governors of Prince Edward Island have always refused to grant a fiat so that in Prince Edward Island we have practically no divorce court. I do not know whether the same condition prevails in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and British Columbia, but, in Prince Edward Island that statute has never been availed of and we have never had any divorces in that province. Any person who has sought a divorce, and I believe there has only been one, has had to come before the Senate Committee at great expense. The expense of a divorce to an applicant from that province would, I believe, be something like $600 or $1,000. I believe that my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) is trying to remedy that condition and to cut down the expense. The Senate is simply a court for the rich man, and the poor man has no show. If the principle of divorce is one which should prevail in this country there should be the same remedy given to all classes. I am not going to express any opinion as to the right of any person to go before any court to get a divorce, but as we have the law, surely something should be done to simplify it, and to give equal rights all our citizens.
