Mr. WILLIAM THOBURN (North Lanark); Mr. Speaker, I was very much interested in the discussion which took place this afternoon on divorce, particularly as I am one of the sub-committee of the Commons that was appointed to attend the Senate Committee meetings on divorce. I am not quite sure whether the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) approves of it or not. Personally, I think it was a step in the right direction. Before the sub-committee was appointed, the usual procedure was for the evidence to be taken before the Senate Committee; it was then printed, and circulated amongst the members of the Private Bills Committee and

the members of the House of Commons. Very few of these gentlemen took the pains to read the evidence, and the consequence was that when the Bill came up little attention was paid to it. For that reason, I think the appointing of the sub-committee was a Step in the right direction.
I heartily agree with the hon. member for East Hastings that there should be some improvement in our system of divorce. But how to go about it is a problem; and as far as I could learn, the hon. member himself did not offer any solution. I would have wished that he had gone a little further in his elucidation of the subject. From my experience I have no hesitation in saying that the power of granting divorces should be removed altogether from the Parliament of Canada, and placed in the law courts. To that extent, I agree with' the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll). A very, very delicate question was touched on this afternoon in connection with church denominations. I confess, as a member of [DOT]the sub-committee, that I was somewhat surprised when I was told that gentlemen of a certain religious persuasion were entirely opposed to granting divorce, on account of the rules of itheir church. It has been stated here this afternoon that more than one denomination is opposed to divorce, and that seems to me to open up a very serious question. If I understand the hon. member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux) aright, I think his statement was to the effect that in certain cases he would rather obey the laws of his church than the laws of Canada. If I have misquoted him, perhaps he will correct me.
I said that on the question of divorce I preferred to follow the judgments of the ecclesiastical courts rather than the judgments of the civil courts.

If that practice became general, where would it land the people of this country? If one denomination has a right to make laws for its members, so has every denomination in the Dominion, and if the members of these different denominations should prefer to obey the laws of their own church rather than the laws of Canada, a very serious state of affairs would develop. That is a question that might be debated in this House for several weeks, and it is one which might cause a tremendous upheaval. It does seem to me
	.
that the laws of Canada should have precedence over the laws of any church.
I wish to give some reasons why I think the power of granting divorces should be taken from Parliament and vested in the law courts of Canada. As the hon. member for Cape Breton said, there are very few members of this House who know the procedure of a divorce suit in Parliament. And let me tell the hon. member for East Hastings that it is not so much a question of cost. Let him reduce the expense of divorce proceedings here to almost any price he pleases, and still there will be danger of injustice as the court is constituted. Here is the procedure, as well as I can remember it. The case goes before the Senate Chamber and it is then relegated to the Senate Committee on Divorce. The hon. member for Cape Breton did not agree with the verdicts given by that committee. That committee is composed of eleven members, if I recollect aright, and among these are some of the brightest minds of the Senate, including some of the ablest lawyers to be found in this country. And, from my experience, I would go so far as to make this suggestion which the hon. member for East Hastings may think it worth while to consider: If divorce is to remain with this Parliament, then let the proceedings end with the Senate Divorce Committee. When the divorce Bill is brought before this House it is relegated to the Private Bills Committee, and before the subcommittee was, appointed, the Private Bills Committee took the evidence in these cases as read, and the same might almost be said when the matter came before the House of Commons. I would like to know how many members of this House ever read the evidence in divorce cases before giving their vote, if they were called upon to vote.
I have a vivid and enduring recollection of one case that came before this House last session, and which had passed the Senate Committee unanimously. Let me tell hon. members that for a divorce Bill to pass that committee the evidence has to be conclusive beyond the shadow of a doubt. This case came before the Private Bills Committee of this House and was there argued pro and con to the best of the ability of those who took part, with the result that the Bill was defeated by a majority of one. The evidence was printed, and the case was considered such a miscarriage of justice that, if I remember well, it was submitted to the Prime Minister, and he voted with others to refer it back to the Private

Bills Committee. Here is where comes in the nefarious work of which I complain, and that is a strong word, but the occasion requires strong words. When it was found that the case had to go back to the Private Bills Committee outside influence was brought in and wire-pulling engaged in. If the case had been before a bench of judges the parties would never have dared to act as they did on that occasion. I stood at the door of the corridor leading to room 16, and saw an individual standing outside that door, button-holing the members as they came out, and using his influence to get them to vote against the applicant for divorce, and this was an individual whose name was actually mentioned as one of the parties implicated. That is why I say it was a nefarious transaction. The result was that when the Bill was sent back to the Private Bills Committee, owing to the influence that had been brought to bear on some of the members, and because they had heard only one side of the question, the Bill was defeated. There were only a certain few members who were familiar with the evidence in the case, but as a result of the canvassing that was done by that individual the Bill was lost. Were the printed evidence submitted to any court of justice in Canada that decision would be reversed.
Reference was made here this afternoon to the law courts and divorce laws of the United States. It does not follow that because divorce procedure in the United States is lax that it should be lax in Canada. We know that there are many laws of the United States the enforcement of which seems to us to be lax. I have too much faith in the judiciary of Canada to be in the least afraid of the results of their decisions if suits for divorce were referred to them. There would be no chance in the world that resort would be had to such tactics as I have spoken of here to-night.
I have given, as plainly as I possibly could, my reasons, based upon personal experience, for holding that divorce cases should be removed from the Parliament of Canada and delegated to the law courts, presided over by at least three judges. I feel satisfied that if this plan were adopted, justice would be done to all persons concerned, and the expense would be small compared with what it is at the present time.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the very clear and logical address of the Minister of Justice, in which he dealt with the history of the law of divorce, both in England and in this country.
There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation 'of 1858 was merely a codification of what was really the common law of England on the subject of divorce. I do not think it will be questioned that the different Acts that were passed by the Imperial Parliament granting divorces to different persons were along even lines: that is, the same principle was recognized throughout in granting these divorces. The Minister of Justice was right when he said that the common law as it was then was not out and out a law, but a custom which was crystallized into a statute in 1858; and the hon. minister did not tell us that in the Statute of 1858 there was anything that was not really the law previous to that year. When the power to enforce the provision, which was put into the form of a statute in 1858, was transferred from the legislature to the courts of the country, I do not think that the law was changed, or that the conditions were changed so far as remedy goes; the rule or custom was simply put in the form of a statute, and its administration was entrusted to the courts instead of the legislature. There is no doubt that a court properly constituted and presided over by one or more learned jurists is more capable of properly administering the law than a mixed assembly of men, some of whom are learned in law and some of whom are not.

I feel that I owe an apology to the House for my failure to express the ideas that were in my mind when I drafted this resolution and when I addressed the House this afternoon. Let me assure you, Sir, that it was not owing to any intentional disrespect, but to my ignorance and to the limitations of my vocabulary. I would have thought, in my innocence and ignorance, that this resolution was reasonably clear and such that a wayfaring man, though a fool, could not err very much in reading it. I hope the House will pardon me if I take the opportunity of reading it now in the hope that some person, perhaps, may be as ignorant and blind as myself, and may also think that it is a reasonably clear resolution. It 's as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the procedure under which divorces are granted by Parliament-
-not by the Senate, but by Parliament.
-and the consequent unreasonable expense thereof, are so unsatisfactory, besides being prohibitive to the great majority of the people of Canada, the same should be taken into immediate consideration by the Government during the present session, with a view to reform.
The expense and the procedure at present are so unreasonable that the Government this session should take the matter into consideration with a view to reform. That
is the whole thing. One hon. gentleman argues from that, that because divorces in the United States have multiplied to a great extent, therefore the same result would follow if there were a reform of our procedure, although everybody knows that in the United States divorces are granted on almost every ground under the sun, and that an enormous negro population greatly increases the percentage of divorces. Another hon. gentleman argued that if my motion were passed it would be an insult to the Senate because, he said, we have no right to arrogate to ourselves the power of reforming their rules. It might be that, if a Committee were appointed and sat, it would find that all the defects existing at the present time were in the procedure of this House, and not in that of the other branch of Parliament. But inasmuch as every member of the House who has spoken has admitted that the procedure is defective, it seems to me a most extraordinary state of affairs that the Minister of Justice, speaking for the Government, should object to doing something to correct what he ' admits to be wrong for fear that the resolution now before the House would be a reflection on the Senate, when there is not even mention of the Senate in the resolution.

That, in the opinion of this House, in order to secure to the farmers and people of Canada the advantages of the American market for wheat, wheat products and potatoes, steps should he taken at once to put these articles on the free list in the Canadian Tariff.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is of sueh paramount importance that I feel I should not be doing my duty to my constituents, and to my province, if I did not bring the subject up once more for debate in this House. This question of securing the American market for the western farmer is one that will not down. My hon. friends on the Government benches may try as hard as they like, but they cannot get rid of this question until a proper solution of it has been found. I remember
that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, at a bye-election in the constituency of Macdonald, a few years ago, practically promised the farmers that they would get free wheat if it was in the interests of the country. Three years have passed by since that day, and, so far as we can judge, the farmers are no nearer free wheat than they were at that time. But we have kept up the agitation, and we will keep it up until we get what we are after. In order, Mr. Speaker, that you may have a just idea of what we are talking about, I want to read to the House definitions of the different grades of Manitoba and Minneapolis wheat, and I want hon. gentlemen opposite to pay particular attention to this, so that they will see that when they quote Number 2 Manitoba Northern against Minneapolis Number 2, they are quoting Manitoba wheat that is always two grades, and sometimes more than two grades, higher than the so-called corresponding wheat at Minneapolis. For instance, Number 3 Manitoba Northern is a much better wheat than Number 2 Minneapolis Northern. Let me read the definitions :
Manitoba . Grades Spring Wheat.
No. 1 Manitoba Hard wheat shall be sound and well cleaned, weighing not less than 60 pounds to the bushel, and shall be composed of at least seventy-five per cent of hard Red Fife wheat.
No. 1 Hard White Fife wheat shall be sound and well cleaned, weighing not less than 60 pounds to the bushel, and shall be composed of not less than sixty per cent of hard White Fife wheat and shall not contain more than twenty-five per cent of soft wheat.
No. 1 Manitoba Northern wheat shall be sound and well cleaned, weighing not less than sixty pounds to the bushel, and shall be composed of at least sixty per cent of hard Red Fife wheat.	.
No. 2 Manitoba Northern wheat, shall be sound and reasonably clean, of good milling qualities and fit for warehousing, weighing nop less than 58 pounds to the bushel, and shall be composed of at least forty-five per cent of hard Red Fife wheat.
Any wheat not good enough to be graded as No. 2 Manitoba Northern shall be graded as No. 3 Manitoba Northern in the discretion of the inspector.
Minnesota Grades, Northern Spring Wheat.
No. 1 Hard Spring wheat shall be sound, bright, sweet and clean, and consist of over fifty per cent of the hard varieties, and weigh not less than 58 pounds to the measured bushel.
No. 1 Northern Spring wheat shall be sound, sweet and clean, and consist of the hard and soft varieties of spring wheat, and weigh not less than 57 pounds to the measured bushel.
No. 2. Northern Spring wheat shall be spring wheat not clean enough nor sound enough for No. 1, but of good milling quality, and may

consist of the bearded varieties, and must not weigh less than 56 pounds to the measured bushel.	.
No. 3 Northern Spring wheat shall be composed of shrunken, inferior spring wheat, and weigh not less than 54 pounds to the measured bushel.
No. 4 Northern Spring wheat shall include all inferior spring wheat that is badly shrunken or damaged, and weigh not less than 49 pounds to the measured bushel.
Rejected Spring wheat shall include all varieties of Spring wheat, sprouted, badly bleached, or for any other cause unfit for No. 4.
So there is quite a difference between the Minneapolis .and Manitoba grades. No. 2 Manitoba Northern must be good milling wheat weighing not less than fifty-eight pounds to the bushel, and must be composed of at least forty-five per cent Red Fife wheat. Any of our wheat that had a less percentage of Red Fife in it than that would be graded as No. 3. Again, American No. 2 Northern has to weigh only fifty-six pounds to the bushel, whereas our so-called corresponding grade has to weigh fifty-eight, American No. 2 Northern need not have any hard wheat at all, while the Manitoba No. 2 must have at least forty-five per cent. I think hon. gentlemen opposite will now see that in quoting No. 2 Manitoba Northern against No. 2 Minneapolis they are comparing absolutely different grades. For instance, our No. 3 Northern is a far better milling wheat than No. 1 Minneapolis, and I say without a possible chance of successful contradiction that in many, cases our No. 3 is a much better milling wheat than No. 1 Minneapolis. It is therefore absolutely unfair to compare No. 3 Manitoba Northern with No. 3 Minneapolis. Our grades are practically confined to 1, 2 and 3 Northern. The grades at Minneapolis are altogether different. Taking into account the difference in the grades and the difference in the price, I make this statement on my responsibility as a member of this House, that for the last twenty years there has not been a single year in which the 'armers of Assiniboia could not, during ten or eleven months out of the year, take their wheat across the line, if it were not for the duty, and get ten to sixteen cents a bushel more for it than they could get at home.
I do not say that they could do that every day in the year, or every week in the year, but, practically speaking, they could do it for ten or eleven months out of the year.
There is another point. In the months of September, October, and November last there was a spread of seven or eight cents a bushel between the Winnipeg and the 
American price, not taking into consideration the difference in grades. But what do we find when the wheat got to Liverpool? Instead of the Manitoba wheat selling for seven or eight cents less a bushel than the American wheat it sold to the Liverpool merchant at from six to eight cents a bushel more than the American wheat, and that cannot be denied by any one who knows anything about the grain trade. Why should there be this difference? Why should every man who grows wheat in Canada be crucified to the extent of ten cents a bushel on his wheat? It was stated during the reciprocity debate that we would be paying too much for reciprocity. I do not believe it. But supposing it were true. Two years ago the United States put wheat on the free list to any country that adopted the same policy with regard to their wheat. All we have to do to secure the American market for the Canadian farmer is to put our wheat on the free list. Why should that not be done? Why does not the Government give our farmers access, to the American market?
The Minister of Finance made this statement the other day:
I always assume that those engaged in a business know the best way of carrying that business on. My hon. friend says quite truly that men can give essays and lectures as to what class of farming should be carried on, but after all the farmer knows best what kind of farming he should engage in. I have always said that.
Further, he said:
I may say, however, that the legislation has been brought forward for no other purpose ' than to meet the needs of a growing industry in the West, as presented to me by the parties engaged in that industry.
The Minister of Finance thought the Farmer knew his own business best, and that the farmer's advice should be followed. Now, if my hon. friends on the Government benches listen to these Western farmers when they ask for an amendment of the Bank Act, why should not they listen to exactly the same association and exactly the same men when they ask the right to sell their own products in the American markets? I will- tell you why. When the farmers ask for an amendment to the Bank Act, it happens to be in the interest of the Bankers' Association, and the Government are quite ready and willing to grant what is asked. But when the demand is made for free wheat, the millers and the dealers jump in and say: we do not want that; and so the Government turn a deaf

ear to the request that is made. If you ask why the interests should be favoured rather than farmers, the only reason I can suggest is that the big interests are. fat subscribers when it comes to raising election funds, and the farmers are lean subscribers.
Last summer I was out in my constituency, and one day I drove into the town of Carievale. I was accompanied by Mr. Burke, and Mr. Little, two well-to-do farmers. We went to the elevators in Carievale and asked the price of wheat. Also we went to an elevator where they sold flour, and asked the price of flour. Then we jumped into an automobile and inside of an hour and a half we were in Sherwood, North Dakota. We went to the elevators there and asked what they were paying for wheat and found that they were paying just 13 cents a bushel more than was being paid on the Canadian side at Carievale. There was a lot of Canadian wheat coming over and paying the duty of ten cents a bushel and making more by selling it in Sherwood than they could make by selling it at home. Why, Mr. Speaker, one of the big elevators in Sherwood, North Dakata is owned by my own constituents, a farmers' elevator. They own it and run it and they ship thousands, and tens of thousands, and some years hundreds of thousands, of bushels of Canadian grain to that elevator, and they send it there because they can get better prices than they can get at home! And hon. members on the other side tell us lhat wheat is lower in the United States than it is in Canada. They tell us also that the United States exports wheat as we do, and. consequently, their market can be of no use to us. I do not care whether the United States exports wheat or not. What I know is that the American elevator man is there with money ready to buy our wheat, and pay a higher price for it than we can get on our side of the line. And that argument of a higher price is good enough for me and for the farmers I represent. On that occasion at Sherwood, we asked also the price of flour, and we found that the best quality of flour-the practical farmers who were with me told me it was practically the same as the best brand of Lake of the Woods and Ogilvie flour on our side-was selling at thirty cents a sack cheaper than we could buy it in Carievale. The American miller pays 13 cents a bushel more for his wheat, and sells his flour at 60 cents 'a barrel less than on our side. Will hon. gentlemen
opposite explain that? I should like the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen), who is great at explanations, to explain that. He may explain it satisfactorily to the hon. members about him, but when they go back to their constituents on the prairies they will find that their explanation is mighty thin, and that it does not explain to the farmer at all, for the simple fact is that the American miller is prepared to pay a higher price for wheat and to take a lower price for flour than the miller on our side. And remember, our farmers are practically all buyers of flour from these big milling concerns. There are practically no small mills doing business in the West. A number have been built, but the majority of them are standing idle to-day. And why? I will tell you: The moment a small mill starts in any of the towns through the West, at once the price of wheat is put up in that particular town, and also they will ship in flour and put its price away down, and they will keep that going for a year, or two years, or three years if necessary, until they have throttled that man and ruined him. Then they can put the price of wheat down and the price of flour up. That is done every day in the week in our country. I leave it to hon. members from the West to say whether it is not the same in their constituencies as it is in mine.
If Canadian wheat were put on the free list and the Canadian farmer given the right to ship to the American market, who would suffer? Let my friends opposite answer this question. The Canadian farmers are asking that wheat be put on the free list; why not grant their request? Let us suppose that the woollen and cotton manufactures came to the Government in a body and said: we have been paying duty on our products long enough; if the duties were taken off cottons and woollens, we should be able to ship a great deal more and get a much better price for our goods. Would the Government turn them down if the farmers should say that they did not want the duty taken off? No, the Government would listen to the demands of the people who were in the business. The Government are prepared to listen to the farmers of the West when they ask for an amendment of the Bank Act, because it is in the interests of the banks that they should do so, but when the farmers ask for an amendment of the Customs Act so that wheat may be put on the free list, the Government say, no. I ask again, who is going to suffer if we have free wheat, except, perhaps, the millers and a few dealers?

Will any other interest suffer? I do not see what other interest can possibly suffer. Why should half a dozen millers have more influence with the Government than all the farmers of Canada? The united farmers of Ontario have asked for free wheat; so have the farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta; and the only reason why their request has not been granted is that the millers and a few dealers have asked that the duty be retained.
I am free to admit that the miller will suffer from any provision for free wheat; he would have to pay more for his wheat and sell his flour at a lower price. A few of the dealers might not get so much wheat to handle, because a considerable quantity would go to the South, and there might be more competition in buying. I do think it is unfair that the interests of a few millers and a few dealers on the Grain Exchange in Winnipeg should overrule the interests of all the farmers of Canada who are asking for free wheat. I venture to say that no man in this House can get a single farmers' organization in the West to pass a motion asking that the duty on wheat be retained. It cannot be done; all the farmers of the West, Conservative as well as Liberal are in favour of free wheat. My hon. friends have been able to shuffle this question in the past, but it is getting more difficult all the time to do this, and if the matter is not soon settled in the interests of the farmers it will be hard for my hon. friends to make a satisfactory explanation of their course. The western farmer is a reasonable man; he does not try to shirk his share of taxation. He demands the right to sell his product in the best market; he is going to have that right, and if this Government will not give it to him, when the time comes there will be a Government in power that will give it to them. I would have my ftiends opposite remember that in the next Parliament there will be sixteen more members from the prairies than there are at the present time; and all of them, Liberal as well as Conservative, will be in favour of putting wheat on the free list. The Minister of Public Works and the Solicitor General are to-day in their hearts as much in favour of free wheat as I am; they know it, and they cannot honestly deny it. They cajoled the people into believing that they were going to give them free wheat, and they have been unable to do if.
It may be said by some that the removal of the duty upon wheat would not be in

the interests of the railways; the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I think-one of the ministers of the Crown, in any case- said that this fact would have to be considered. Well, Mr. Lanigan, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, made the statement two or three months ago that the putting of wheat on the free list would not particularly affect the railways. I happened to have some interviews with the Railway Commission quite recently, and they told me that all the railroads were so tied up that they would be glad to see wheat go into the United States in order that the blockade might be relieved.
Has the hon. gentleman Mr. Lanigan's statement?

Yes; I shall be very
pleased to give it. I quote from the Grain Growers' Guide-my hon. friend the Solicitor General-knows that paper-of December 1 last, page 9:
Free Wheat Won't Hurt Railroads.
Some of the politicians who are opposed to free wheat have stated that they are against opening the United States market to Canadian farmers because it would send all our wheat south and leave the tracks of the three Canadian transcontinental railroads to become mere streaks of rust.
What fools we Canadians must have been to spend a thousand million dollars in building three Canadian railroad lines when, merely by putting wheat on the free list, we shall make them mere streaks of rust. That is kind of argument my hon. friends opposite are advancing. This article goes on to say:
That would, of course, be serious if it were true, but W. B. Lanigan, an important and well-informed official of the Canadian Pacific railway, says is is not so. In the Manitoba Free Press of November 24 was the following:
Will Equalize Prices. Lanigan Says Free Wheat
Will not Affect Canadian Pacific railway.
Free wheat would have no effect on the amount of hauling done by the Canadian Pacific railway according to W. B. Lanigan, assistant freight traffic manager. Mr. Lanigan explained the statement by saying that free wheat would equalize the prices in Canada and in the United States. Then there would be little or no incentive to ship grain south.
That is exactly what we have always claimed.	[DOT]

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would be interested to know that, he is quoting the Free Press and the Guide, instead of Mr. Lanigan. I wrote to Mr. Lanigan with regard to that statement,

and I have a letteT from him to the effect that he gave no such statement.

Give us free wheat and the farmer who grows the wheat will get a better price and the man who is working at $1.50 or $2 or $2.50, with a big family to feed and support, will buy his flour cheaper so that it works both ways. I say that the mechanic can buy his flour cheaper. He can go into any market in the United States and buy flour cheaper than he can buy our flour made from our western wheat. Does anyone tell me that concerns like the Ogilvy Milling Company, the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, the Western Milling Company, the Maple Leaf Milling Company, with the greatest waterpowers in the world, cannot make flour as cheaply as the American millers? Our millers have the greatest water-powers in the world. For one horse-power in the United States our millers have one hundred horse-power available. We have the cheapest and best water-powers, we have the best wheat on earth, we have as able men in the milling business as stand on the face of this globe; and will anyone tell me that with all these advantaged the Canadian miller cannot hold his own against the American? He can do it but he does not want to do it.
I do not blame him for not, wanting to. As- long as he can get this Government to stand between himself and competition, why .should he not do so? Why should he not save ten or fifteen cents a bushel on his wheat and chisel the consumer out of fifty cents a barrel on the flour if he can do it and can have the Government look after him in that way so that he can rob the people to that extent? That is what the millers are doing, they are robbing the farmer on one hand and the consumer on the other-and this Government is upholding them in doing so. The millers could not do this for one moment without the assistance of this Government. The people of the West know this and the consumers of the East are beginning to learn it. Give us free wheat and you will satisfy everybody except the millers and a few dealers. You will save millions of dollars to the growers of the wheat, and you will make a great big saving to the men who have to buy the flour. If that is not a good argument why we should have free wheat I do not know what you would consider a good argument. There is no question that it is simply because this Government refuses to go against the wishes and the demands of the big in-

terests that they refuse to take action in this matter. A few months ago, when the crop was seen to be so large for the American market, the Government wavered as to whether or not they should grant the demand then made. But what did the millers tell them ? They said: You give free wheat, and then we will demand free machinery for our mills, free bags to put our flour in, and free everything that we use in the mill. The Government listened to the seductive voice of the big interests, but the demands of the farmers were of no avail whatever; the Government turned a deaf ear to them. As I said before, this is a matter that will have to be settled with the farmers the next time the Government go to the country.
Before I take up the question of the . millers, however, let me give you a quotation of the prices at Sherwood, the town in North Dakota that I spoke of a few minutes ago. I have the resolution here, copies of which some farmers- in my constituency sent- to the Prime Minister, to myself, and to the Grain Growers' Association. This resolution was p-assed by the Elmore and Fife Association on December 29, 1915. I will take the prices for the previous four months. On September 15 bonded wheat was 75 cents, and domestic wheat 86 cents, a difference of 11 cents per bushel. On October 15 bonded wheat was 83 cents, and domestic wheat 86 cents, only 3 cents better. On November 15 bonded wheat was 81 cents, and domestic wheat 89 cents, a spread of 8 cents. On December 15 bonded' wheat was 88 cents, and domestic wheat 98 cents, a difference of 10 cents per bushel. And this was at the time of the year when some of the papers were pointing out that wheat was higher in Winnipeg than it was in Minneapolis. No doubt there will be certain days when the price of wheat will be higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis, but does that prove anything? If, on one day in twenty, wheat is higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis, does that imply that the Minneapolis market is no good for us, when, on the other 19 days, there is a difference of 5, 10 or 12 cents a bushel in favour of Minneapolis? My hon. friends opposite must think the farmers are a lot of thick-headed fools if they assume that they would send their wheat to Minneapolis and take a lower price than they could get at home for it. Does anyone believe that the farmers would do that? Does anyone believe that a Canadian farmer would ship a carload of wheat to

Minneapolis if he could get a better price at home? If he can get as much at home for his wheat as at Minneapolis he will sell his wheat at home every time. If the Government believes that wheat is worth more in Winnipeg than it is in the United States, why not give the Canadian farmers what they want, because it will not do anybody any harm? It will not affect the market to the extent of the sale of a bushel of grain because the Canadian farmer will sell at home if the market is equal to the best he can get. But during September, October, and November, the farmers of the West lost over $10,000,000 in not being able to have the American market for their wheat. The Government would not give them the American market, they sent their wheat to the old country, and the farmer is paying from 40 cents to 45 cents a bushel to take his wheat from tide water to Liverpool. For the munition manufacturers who were able to charge this and the British Government four prices for their goods, they could get a rate which was practically the same as the rate before the war, but the rate for carrying wheat which, before the war, was from 5 to 7 cents a bushel, went up to from 40 to 45 cents a bushel. The Government were either powerless or careless, or they did not have the interest of the farmers at heart to the same degree that they had the interest of the manufacturers, they did not give them the American market and they allowed them to be robbed on this last year's crop to the extent of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 in excessive freight rates.
That is the position that the farmer is in. Is it any wonder that he is demanding free wheat? The wonder is that any bunch of men could be got together who would refuse it. The wonder is that any Government would refuse such a reasonable demand from the people as that they be allowed to sell their wheat in the best way they could. What I say about wheat applies to wheat products and potatoes. If potatoes were put on the free list the American market would prove most profitable to the Canadian farmer who grows potatoes. We, in the West, do not grow potatoes to any considerable extent, not that we cannot grow them and grow them in abundance, but because there has never been a market. In my own constituency one year a man put in fifteen acres of potatoes and bought the necessary machinery to handle them. He had a large crop, he wrote to Winnipeg and the best price
he could get left him only six cents a bushel for the potatoes loaded on the cars, after buying the sacks to put them in and paying the freight rate. He sent a man down into the United States and he sold these potatoes, consisting of fifteen or twenty car loads at St. Louis. I cannot remember the exact figures but after paying the duty he had the big price of 30 or 40 cents a bushel for his potatoes. However, as I said, we do not grow potatoes up there because we have no steady market. If we had the American market for potatoes we could grow them profitably.
It is the same with our cattle. Formerly the-prices kept going up and down all the time. Every little while there would be a combination of the buyers, and the price would go down. Prices have been steady and higher ever since we had the American market for our cattle. They ought to take it tomorrow, I know, but I do not anticipate that they will do it as soon as that. The Government had the opportunity to save the farmers from loss early last fall. They had the right, by Order in Council, to put wheat on the free list. In order to make that clear, I had better read the clauses of the Acts. Section 92 of the Consolidated Revenue Act reads as follows:
The Governor in Council whenever he deems it right and conducive to the public good may remit any duty or toll payable to His Majesty, imposed or authorized to be imposed by any Act of the Parliament of Canada.
If that clause was not sufficient, there is another clause that would have enabled my hon. friends opposite to have put wheat on the free list had they been so inclined. The hon. Minister of Public Works went up through the West and told the people there that he had an open mind on the subject. It was well pointed out by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that the farmers were much more interested in having an open market than in having an open mind. It takes my hon. friend's mind a long time to get fully opened, because I remember having heard him three years ago telling the farmers that free wheat was all right. In view of that statement, he believed that they were going to have it right away. However, he has not made much progress in three years, and his mind is still open. Here is another clause under which the Government could have acted. It is section 286 of the Customs Act, and it reads as follows:
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, and in the manner hereinafter provided in addition to the other purposes and matters in this Act mentioned, make regulations for or relating to the following purposes and matters:
" (k) Transferring to the list of goods which may be imported into Canada free of duty, any or all articles, whether natural products on products of manufacturers, used as materials in Canadian manufactures; any such materials transferred to the free list by such Order in Council, to be free of duty of customs for the/ time therein appointed for that purpose."
The Government could have passed an Act this session, but it is now almost too late. Already over two hundred million bushels have gone east of Winnipeg, that is, seven-fifteenths of the crop. Still, even at this hour, the Government could give some relief to the farmers who have not sold their

wheat. At all events a measure of relief passed now would encourage the farmer to grow another large crop next year. Hon. gentlemen opposite sometimes advance the argument that England is our natural market. Now, England consumes about three hundred million bushels of wheat a year. Of that, she grows about sixty million bushels. That leaves about two hundred and forty million bushels which she imports every year. How would the most loyal man on the opposite side of this House say that England would import all that amount from Canada? I do not think any hon. gentleman opposite would say so. England buys in the best market. She sends her ships to every country in the world, and will any one tell me that England would send a ship to the Argentine Republic, unload it there, and then have the ship come up to Halifax or Montreal for a load of Canadian wheat for England. England did not become rich by doing business on those lines, but by buying in the cheapest market and selling in the dearest. Why is it that we have to pay such high freight rates-and I am speaking of freight rates in ordinary times, not war times. One of the reasons is that we impose a high duty on British goods entering this country. Let the Government take off this duty, if they will not give us free wheat, and then we shall import goods from Great Britain, and send the ships back to the Old Country laden with Canadian wheat. England will then be our market, and in that way we will get reasonable freight rates. But the Government will do neither one thing nor the other. They are like the dog in the manger. They will not give us the American market, nor will they take off the duty on British goods, so as to give us cheaper freight rates and a better price to the farmer.
